stem: An RN assesses a previously functioning arteriovenous fistula used for hemodialysis and finds no palpable thrill and no audible bruit. Which complication is most concerning?

options.B: Fistula thrombosis with loss of patency
options.D: Central venous stenosis causing venous hypertension

rationale: A functioning hemodialysis arteriovenous fistula should have evidence of flow, including a palpable thrill and bruit. NCBI StatPearls identifies loss of thrill as a finding associated with acute thrombosis and notes that a thrill implies fistula patency. Therefore, absence of both the thrill and bruit in a previously functioning access is most concerning for thrombosis with loss of patency. A is more typically associated with erythema, warmth, edema, or drainage. C causes distal ischemic manifestations such as pain or altered motor/sensory function rather than isolated loss of fistula flow findings. D commonly causes venous-hypertension findings such as arm swelling, cannulation problems, or increased venous pressures rather than complete disappearance of the expected thrill and bruit.
educational_objective: Recognize loss of the expected thrill and bruit in a hemodialysis AV fistula as an urgent finding suggesting loss of access patency, commonly from thrombosis.

source_locator: Dialysis Fistula > Complications: loss of thrill secondary to acute thrombosis; thrombosis as a major fistula complication. Dialysis Fistula > Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Monitoring: a thrill implies patency; infection findings include erythema/warmth/edema/drainage; steal syndrome causes distal pain or motor/sensory changes; central venous stenosis can cause extremity swelling/cannulation problems/increased venous pressures. Nursing Admission Assessment and Examination > Physical Examination: assess a hemodialysis fistula for thrill or bruit and notify the treating clinician immediately if findings are absent.
source_claim_supported: Loss of expected fistula flow findings, particularly the thrill/bruit, indicates loss of patency and may reflect acute thrombosis; competing access complications have different characteristic assessment findings.

correction_summary: Replaced generic NCBI citation and weak filler distractors with exact NCBI fistula-assessment/complication locators and four authentic vascular-access complications. Tightened the stem to a previously functioning fistula so loss of thrill/bruit clearly represents new loss of patency.
audit_findings: Exact NCBI locators directly support thrill as a patency sign, loss of thrill with acute thrombosis, and the differentiating manifestations of infection, steal syndrome, and central venous stenosis. A-D audit: B uniquely explains disappearance of both expected flow findings; A, C, and D are plausible fistula complications but have different source-supported assessment patterns. The stem avoids assuming a newly created or immature fistula by specifying previously functioning access. No unsupported numerical threshold or procedural rule is introduced. The NCBI nursing assessment source independently supports immediate escalation when thrill/bruit are absent. Blueprint is an exact NCSBN 2026 Physiological Adaptation match.
